status_key.verified: stated in a contemporary document (S1 letters / S4 official chronicle) and consistent with other sources
status_key.corroborated: stated by two or more independent sources, at least one near-contemporary
status_key.tradition: found in later chronicles (Maratha bakhars, Khafi Khan) without contemporary confirmation; narrated with attribution
status_key.disputed: sources conflict; narration states the conflict
status_key.framing: editorial framing, not a factual claim about a specific event

claims.claim: In August 1666 Shivaji was held under guard in Agra with his son.

sources.passage: Round Shiva's residence a patrol of the Emperor's troops has been posted ... Ballu Sah to Kalyandas, Agra, 18 August 1666: This morning Shivaji was found to have fled away from Agra.

claims.claim: One letter from Agra describes the watch as a thousand men.

sources.loc: p. 201, Parkal-das to Meghraj, Agra, 3 September 1666
sources.passage: the news came that Shiva had escaped . . . . from within the thousand men of the watch around him.

claims.note: Single letter; narrated as 'one letter ... puts the watch at a thousand men'.

claims.claim: Sambhaji was nine years old.

sources.passage: His son is nine years old and very marvellously handsome in appearance

claims.claim: The escape was discovered in the morning.

sources.passage: This morning Shivaji was found to have fled away from Agra.
When the day was four gharis old, the news came that Shiva had escaped
It was the ninth hour of the day ... they went into the room to see (but) then, there was no one on the cot.

claims.note: Letters (contemporary) say morning; Sabhasad says afternoon. Scene s14 narrates the conflict.

claims.claim: Letters written in Agra in 1666 survive and allow the legend to be checked.

sources.passage: The body of letters written by the officers of Kumar Ram Singh ... has been traced ... in the Jaipur State archieves in the year 1939.

claims.claim: Shivaji built a kingdom from hill forts in western India and had raided Mughal territory for years (e.g. sack of Surat, January 1664).

sources.passage: From 6th to 10th January he looted the city of Surat

claims.claim: Mirza Raja Jai Singh, Aurangzeb's general, arranged Shivaji's visit.

sources.passage: Jai Singh had undertaken to send Shivaji to the imperial Court ... used a thousand devices ... to induce him to go to Agra.
As Raja Jai Singh had sent Shiva to the Court

claims.claim: Treaty of Purandar (1665): 23 forts annexed to the empire; 12 forts including Rajgad left to Shivaji.

sources.passage: That 23 of his forts ... should be annexed to the empire ; and (b) that 12 of his forts, including Rajgarh ... should be left to Shiva

claims.claim: Jai Singh swore Shivaji would not be harmed; Ram Singh pledged his word at court.

sources.passage: Jai Singh took the most solemn oaths possible for a Hindu that Shiva would not be harmed during his visit, while the Rajput Rajah's son and agent at Court, Kumar Ram Singh, similarly pledged his word
he has come here under a guarantee of safety [from my father]

claims.claim: Shivaji left Rajgad in March 1666 with Sambhaji.

sources.passage: took leave of his family at Rajgarh, and began his journey to Northern India, about the third week of March, 1666, with his eldest son Shambhuji

claims.claim: His contingent at Agra was small but splendidly equipped.

sources.passage: Shivaji has come with a rather small contingent, but with great splendour of equipment.

claims.note: Sabhasad gives 4,000 troops for the journey; Sarkar (S2 p.155 fn) thinks 1,000 more probable. Script avoids a number.

claims.claim: Eyewitness description: lean, short, fair, bearded; 'one does feel instinctively that he is a ruler of men.'

sources.passage: At sight Shivaji's body looks lean and short. His appearance is wonderfully fair in complexion, and even without finding out who he is, one does feel instinctively that he is a ruler of men. ... wears a beard.

claims.note: Quoted from Sarkar's English translation of a Rajasthani letter.

claims.claim: Audience on 12 May 1666, the emperor's 50th lunar birthday.

sources.passage: On Saturday, the 12th May, 1666 ... the Emperor was weighed on his 50th lunar birthday. Shiva with his son Sambha was honoured with an audience.
It was the Emperor's birthday

claims.claim: Shivaji presented gifts of gold coins (nazar).

sources.passage: Shivaji presented one thousand mohars and two thousand rupees as his nazar
He presented 1500 ashrafi as nazar and 6,000 rupees as nisar.

claims.note: Amounts differ between sources; script says 'gifts of gold' only.

claims.claim: The emperor did not speak to him.

sources.passage: The Emperor neither talked with him nor addressed any word to him.

claims.claim: He was placed behind rows of other nobles.

sources.passage: He found himself standing behind several rows of nobles who almost shut him from the Emperor's view.
Shivaji was made to stand in the place of Tahir Khan, in front of Rajah Rai Singh.

claims.claim: Robes of honour went to princes, the chief minister Jafar Khan, and Jaswant Singh.

sources.passage: the khilats for the occasion were presented to the princes, to Jafar Khan (the grand wazir) and to Rajah Jaswant Singh. At this Shiva became sad and fretful

claims.claim: Jaswant Singh had besieged Shivaji's fort of Kondana (1663-64) and failed.

sources.passage: Jaswant, after wasting some months before the fort, delivered a rash and fruitless assault ... The campaign ended with absolutely no gain.

claims.claim: Shivaji said 'I cast off your mansab', turned his back on the throne and walked away.

sources.passage: I cast off your mansab. ... After saying this, he then and there turned his back [to the throne] and roughly walked away.

claims.note: Quoted from Sarkar's translation of a contemporary Rajasthani letter by Ram Singh's staff.

claims.claim: An English (East India Company) report described nobles waiting 'with their hands before them, like mutes'.

sources.passage: His spirit could not bear such humiliation as the other Umaras to wait at a distance with their hands before them, like mutes.
(Surat to Karwar.)

claims.claim: He refused the robe of honour brought by officials.

sources.passage: I refuse to accept the khilat.

claims.claim: Jahanara (Begam Sahib), Jafar Khan and Jaswant Singh urged punishment.

sources.passage: The Begam Sahib, Jafar Khan, and Rajah Jaswant Singh had spoken to the Emperor against Shiva ... [fn] assigned by Shah Jahan to Begum Sahib Jahanara.

claims.claim: The emperor considered killing Shivaji or confining him in a fortress.

sources.passage: Then it came into the Emperor's heart ... either to kill Shiva or to confine him in a fortress, or to throw him into prison.

claims.note: Reported intention per letter writers; narrated as 'a letter from Agra reports'.

claims.claim: Ram Singh argued the emperor should kill him first; the emperor demanded a security bond.

sources.passage: it is proper that the Emperor should first kill me and then only ... Ask Kumar Ram Singh if he will stand security for Shiva, so that if Shiva escapes or does any mischief, the Kumar will take responsibility

claims.claim: Ram Singh signed the bond; a Kabul posting was ordered, then rescinded after petitions and payments.

sources.passage: the Kumar signed the security bond ... Go to Kabul with Shiva ... Shivaji has paid some money to Jafar Khan ... the Emperor has rescinded the order posting him to Kabul.

claims.claim: Fulad Khan's troops guarded the quarters; Ram Singh's Rajputs watched his bed.

sources.passage: The Kumar's men are keeping a watch over Shivaji [in addition to the Kotwal's troops] ... Tej Singh and his retainers keep watch over the bed of Shivaji
Fulad Khan, the police chief of Agra, by imperial order placed a large guard with artillery round Shiva's mansion

claims.claim: Offers and requests: two crore rupees for his forts; to fight against Bijapur; another residence; to become a mendicant at Benares; reply: live in Allahabad fort under watch.

sources.passage: If your Majesty restores to me all my forts taken by you, I shall pay you two krores ... Let me go there, fight and die ... Issue orders for a residence for me ... asking permission to go to Benares ... 'Let him turn faqir and live in Allahabad fort. Bahadur Khan ... will keep a good watch over him!'

claims.claim: c. July 1666 Jai Singh advised that it was 'not at all politic' to let Shivaji return and that he be detained 'in a worthy manner'.

sources.passage: Under the present circumstances it is not at all politic to permit him to come to this region. Also tell the Emperor that Shiva should be detained there in a worthy manner
it is iiot at all politic to send him to this side. Please detain him

claims.claim: Shivaji borrowed Rs 66,000 from Ram Singh around mid-July.

sources.passage: By the middle of July ... he appealed to Kumar Ram Singh, who advanced him Rs. 66,000

claims.claim: He sent his servants and escort home over the summer (from 7 June; escort left c. 25 July).

sources.passage: On Friday, 7 June, Shivaji sent all his servants away ... Shivaji's escort and officers on their return journey crossed the Narwar pass about 15 August, and must have left Agra about 25 July.

claims.claim: He feigned illness and sent out baskets of sweets carried on poles by two porters; guards checked at first and later let them pass.

sources.passage: He feigned illness and began to send out of his house every evening sweetmeats for Brahmans, religious mendicants and courtiers. These were carried in huge baskets slung from a pole which was borne by two men ... The guards searched the baskets for some days and then allowed them to pass out unchallenged.
employing two porters for each basket ... They opened one or two (baskets) (and) found (there were) really sweets. Then (they) let (them) pass.
sent several times each week large covered baskets of sweetmeats
This artful cheat feigning sickness fled with his son

claims.claim: Escape in the third week of August 1666 (17-19 Aug by different sources).

sources.passage: Agra, 18 August 1666. This morning Shivaji was found to have fled
fled with his son on Sunday, the 19th August/27th Safar
(August 29, 1666)

claims.note: Narration says 'one evening in the third week of August' and quotes the dated 18 August letter.

claims.claim: Decoy: Hiroji Farzand lay in Shivaji's bed with one arm visible wearing his gold bracelet; a boy massaged his feet; Shivaji and son left in baskets.

sources.passage: dressed Hiroji Farzand (in them) and made him sleep on his cot. His uncovered hand alone was left visible outside ... a boy was kept for massaging (his limbs).
His half-brother Hiraji Farzand, who looked somewhat like him ... outstretched right arm adorned with Shiva's gold wristlet

claims.note: Narrated as 'According to later accounts'. Not in the contemporary letters.

claims.claim: Chronicles say the decoy held most of the next day; contemporary letters say discovery came that morning.

sources.passage: For four quarters (prahars) of the night, and three quarters of the next day, he lay like that.
This morning Shivaji was found to have fled away from Agra.

claims.claim: Ram Singh's agent urged that paths and river crossings be watched and anyone dressed as a jogi or sannyasi be questioned.

sources.passage: please issue parwanas that watch should be kept at all the paths and ghats ... If any one in the garb of a jogi or sannyasi passes that way, he should be questioned and searched.

claims.claim: Fulad Khan reported the escape happened on Ram Singh's side of the watch; Ram Singh's men were threatened into saying he helped; some withdrew it as made in fear; the emperor cut Ram Singh's rank and took his lands.

sources.passage: Fulad Khan made an outburst of violence and had it reported to the Emperor that Shiva had escaped from the side of the Kumar's patrols. Hence, the Emperor has got angry and ordered the Kumar's rank [mansab] to be reduced, and all the parganas ... taken away ... they had made the confession in fear of torture
Thereupon, Kumar Ram Singh was dismissed from his mansab.

claims.claim: About two weeks later a letter said he had slipped out 'by crouching down in the baskets'.

sources.loc: p. 201, Parkal-das to Meghraj, Agra, 3 September 1666
sources.passage: Afterwards it became known that he had slipped out by crouching down in the baskets [of sweetmeats] which used to be sent out

claims.note: The letter reports what 'became known'; it is not an eyewitness account.

claims.claim: Later Mughal and Maratha histories tell the basket story; the Mughal court suspected inside help; Manucci claimed Ram Singh arranged it.

sources.passage: the Raje and his son crouched in a basket
K. K. ii. 198-201 (most detailed)
Shiva Ji, on the advice of Ram Singh ... sent several times each week large covered baskets
pressed them to make a confession that Kumar Ram Singh had collusively let Shiva escape

claims.claim: Later tradition told of a long pilgrimage route (Allahabad, Benares, Gaya, Puri) in disguise as ascetics.

sources.passage: he travelled eastwards to Mathura, Allahabad, Benares, Gaya, and Puri ... smeared themselves with ashes like Hindu ascetics
besmeared their bodies with ashes and putting on the disguise of Fakirs went towards Muttra.

claims.claim: Letters found in 1939 report spies saying he reached his fort 25 days after slipping out; Sarkar called the pilgrimage tales fiction and inferred fast travel by obscure paths; Shivaji lay ill for weeks.

sources.passage: Shivaji reached home (Rajgarh) only twenty-five days after escaping from his Agra prison, and that he lay severely ill for some weeks after ... We must therefore now discard as pure fiction all the stories told by Khafi Khan and others ... Allahabad, Benares and Gaya—and even Jagannath-Puri

claims.note: 25 days comes from spy reports relayed in a 19 Nov 1666 letter; Sarkar's note gives c. 12 September 1666. Straight-line Agra-Rajgad distance computed as ~1,088 km.

claims.claim: Sambhaji left at Mathura with a Brahmin family; spy reports said the son died on the way; he later returned disguised as a Brahmin relative.

sources.passage: they agreed to keep Shambhuji ... carrying Shambhuji, disguised as a Brahman kinsman
that his son who accompanied him had died on the way

claims.note: Mathura detail from Maratha accounts (narrated as such); death report is contemporary hearsay, narrated as a rumour.

claims.claim: By 1670 Shivaji retook forts ceded at Purandar (e.g. Kondana, Purandar).

sources.passage: during 1670 the Marathas gained Kondana, Purandar, Trimbak, Rohira, Mahuli, Lohgarh

claims.claim: Crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad on 6 June 1674.

sources.passage: Next day (6th June, 1674) came the coronation itself.

claims.claim: Sayings attributed to Aurangzeb lament that the flight of Shivaji, due to carelessness, involved him in campaigns to the end of his days.

sources.passage: See, the flight of the wretch Shiva was due to carelessness, but it has involved me in all these distracting campaigns to the end of my days.

claims.note: Narrated as 'attributed to Aurangzeb' because the Anecdotes collection's authorship is not firmly established.

claims.claim: Ram Singh later led a Mughal campaign in Assam and was defeated at Saraighat (1671) by the Ahom general Lachit Borphukan.

sources.loc: Ram Singh I; Battle of Saraighat
sources.passage: The Battle of Saraighat was a naval battle fought in 1671 ... Mughal commander Ram Singh I ... Ahom commander Lachit Borphukan
sent to join the army fighting in Assam

claims.claim: The Mughal Empire was one of the richest empires on earth.
claims.note: General framing for a broad audience; not tied to a specific statistic.
